subject: biology
overview: This unit applies biology to human welfare. It covers how diseases are caused and spread, how the immune system defends the body, cancer, AIDS and substance abuse, and how microbes are used in food, industry, sewage treatment, energy generation and agriculture. NEET reliably draws 4-6 questions from it. Most are direct, NCERT-based factual questions on pathogen and disease pairs, immunity types, drug sources and microbe-product pairs, so precise recall gives quick marks.

topics.explanation: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease. It depends on genetic factors, infections, lifestyle (food, water, rest, exercise, habits) and a balanced mind. Diseases are infectious if they pass from one person to another, such as typhoid, malaria and AIDS. They are non-infectious if they do not, such as cancer. Pathogens are disease-causing organisms: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans and helminths. Most are parasites, living in or on the host and harming it. A pathogen must enter the body, multiply and interfere with normal function, and it must adapt to the host environment (for example, intestinal pathogens resist stomach acid and digestive enzymes). Spread occurs through contaminated food and water, air (droplets), direct contact or vectors such as mosquitoes and houseflies.
key_points: Health = physical + mental + social well-being.
Infectious diseases spread between people; non-infectious diseases such as cancer do not.
Cancer is a major non-infectious cause of death.
Pathogen groups: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, helminths.
Most pathogens are parasites that harm the host.
Modes of transmission: air, water, food, contact and vectors.
Good health is maintained by a balanced diet, personal hygiene, sanitation, vaccination and vector control.
topics.neet_tip: NEET asks you to classify diseases as infectious or non-infectious and to identify the pathogen group (bacterial, viral, protozoan, fungal or helminth).
topics.topic: Health and disease; pathogens and parasites

topics.explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium (P. vivax, P. malariae, P. falciparum; falciparum causes the most serious, malignant form). Sporozoites enter through the bite of a female Anopheles mosquito. They multiply asexually first in liver cells and then in RBCs. Rupture of RBCs releases the toxin haemozoin, which causes chills and high fever recurring every 3-4 days. Gametocytes form in RBCs. Fertilisation and development occur in the mosquito gut, and sporozoites are stored in the mosquito's salivary glands. Filariasis (elephantiasis) is caused by Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi, transmitted by female mosquitoes, and causes chronic inflammation of lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs and genitals. Ascariasis is caused by Ascaris and spreads through contaminated food and water. Typhoid is caused by Salmonella typhi and is confirmed by the Widal test. Pneumonia is caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. Common cold is caused by rhinoviruses. Amoebiasis is caused by Entamoeba histolytica, with houseflies as mechanical carriers. Ringworm is caused by Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton. Dengue and chikungunya are viral and spread by Aedes mosquitoes.
key_points: Malaria: Plasmodium is a protozoan; the female Anopheles is the vector and the definitive host.
Humans are the intermediate host of Plasmodium; asexual reproduction occurs in liver cells and RBCs.
Haemozoin causes the cyclic chills and fever of malaria.
Filariasis: Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi; the worms live in lymphatic vessels and cause elephantiasis of the limbs and genitals.
Ascariasis: internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia and blockage of the intestinal passage; eggs pass out in faeces.
Typhoid: sustained high fever of 39-40 degrees C, weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite.
Typhoid can cause intestinal perforation and death; it is diagnosed by the Widal test.
Mary Mallon (Typhoid Mary) was a symptomless carrier of typhoid.
Pneumonia infects the alveoli, which fill with fluid; lips and fingernails may turn grey to bluish.
Pneumonia spreads by droplets and by sharing glasses or utensils.
Common cold: rhinoviruses infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs; it lasts 3-7 days.
Amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery): Entamoeba histolytica lives in the large intestine.
Amoebiasis symptoms: constipation, abdominal pain, cramps, and stools with excess mucus and blood clots.
Ringworm: dry, scaly, itchy lesions on skin, nails and scalp; heat and moisture favour it, especially in groin and skin folds.
Dengue and chikungunya: viral diseases with fever and joint pain, spread by Aedes; control by eliminating stagnant water.
topics.neet_tip: Expect pathogen-disease-vector matching and malaria life-cycle statements, such as where sexual and asexual stages occur.
topics.topic: Human diseases: malaria, filariasis, ascariasis, typhoid, pneumonia, common cold, amoebiasis, ringworm, dengue, chikungunya

topics.explanation: Immunity is the ability of the host to fight pathogens. Innate immunity is non-specific and present at birth. It has four types of barrier: physical (skin, mucus), physiological (stomach acid, saliva, tears), cellular (neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, NK cells) and cytokine (interferons protect uninfected cells from viruses). Acquired immunity is pathogen-specific and has memory. The first encounter produces a low-intensity primary response; a later encounter produces a stronger, faster secondary (anamnestic) response. B-lymphocytes produce antibodies, giving humoral immunity. T-lymphocytes give cell-mediated immunity (CMI), which is responsible for graft rejection. An antibody is a Y-shaped molecule of two heavy and two light chains. Active immunity is slow and comes from the body's own response to antigens (infection or vaccine). Passive immunity is quick and comes from ready-made antibodies (colostrum IgA, placental IgG, antitoxin and antivenom). Vaccines work by creating memory B and T cells. Allergy is an exaggerated IgE response with release of histamine and serotonin from mast cells. Autoimmunity, such as rheumatoid arthritis, is an attack on self cells.
key_points: Antibody types: IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG and IgM.
IgG crosses the placenta; IgA is abundant in colostrum; IgE mediates allergy; IgM is the largest antibody (pentamer).
Primary lymphoid organs are bone marrow and thymus, where lymphocytes form and mature.
Secondary lymphoid organs: spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix and MALT.
MALT makes up about 50 percent of the body's lymphoid tissue.
The thymus is large at birth and shrinks with age.
The spleen is a large bean-shaped organ that filters blood and acts as a reservoir of erythrocytes.
Recombinant DNA technology produces hepatitis B vaccine in yeast.
Allergens include dust mites, pollen and animal dander; allergy is treated with antihistamines, adrenalin and steroids.
Snakebite is treated with antivenom containing preformed antibodies, which gives passive immunity.

formulas.meaning: Antibody structure: two heavy and two light polypeptide chains forming a Y shape.

topics.neet_tip: NEET favours questions on antibody types and locations, primary versus secondary lymphoid organs, active versus passive immunity, and innate barrier examples.
topics.topic: Basic concepts of immunology and vaccines

topics.explanation: Normal cells show contact inhibition: they stop dividing when they touch other cells. Cancer cells lose this property and divide uncontrollably to form tumours. Benign tumours stay localised and cause little damage. Malignant tumours invade surrounding tissue, and cells that reach distant sites through the blood start new tumours there, a process called metastasis. Cancer-causing agents (carcinogens) include ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays), non-ionising UV radiation, chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, and oncogenic viruses. Cellular oncogenes (c-onc), or proto-oncogenes, can become activated and transform cells. Cancer is detected by biopsy and histopathological study, by blood and bone marrow tests (for leukaemia), and by imaging: radiography, CT and MRI. Monoclonal antibodies against cancer-specific antigens are also used. Treatment combines surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and immunotherapy.
key_points: Cancer cells have lost contact inhibition.
Benign tumours are non-invasive; malignant tumours are invasive and metastasise.
Ionising carcinogens: X-rays and gamma rays; non-ionising: UV radiation.
Oncogenic viruses carry viral oncogenes.
MRI uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation.
CT uses X-rays to produce 3-D images.
Biological response modifiers such as alpha-interferon activate the immune system against tumours.
Chemotherapy has side effects such as hair loss and anaemia.
topics.neet_tip: NEET asks about carcinogen types, the meaning of metastasis, detection techniques (especially MRI versus CT) and alpha-interferon therapy.

topics.explanation: AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) was first reported in 1981. It is caused by HIV, a retrovirus with an RNA genome inside an envelope. HIV spreads through sexual contact with an infected person, transfusion of contaminated blood, sharing of infected needles (common among intravenous drug users), and from an infected mother to her child through the placenta. After entry, the virus infects macrophages. Its reverse transcriptase copies the viral RNA into DNA, which integrates into the host DNA, so the macrophage becomes an 'HIV factory'. HIV then enters helper T-lymphocytes (TH cells), replicates and destroys them, progressively lowering the TH count. The patient becomes immunodeficient and suffers opportunistic infections such as Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and Toxoplasma. The period between infection and AIDS symptoms is 5-10 years. Diagnosis is by ELISA. Antiretroviral drugs prolong life but do not cure the disease. Prevention relies on safe blood, disposable needles, condoms and awareness.
key_points: HIV is a retrovirus; its genetic information flows from RNA to DNA via reverse transcriptase.
Macrophages act as the HIV factory; helper T cells are the main cells killed.
The incubation period is 5-10 years.
ELISA is the standard diagnostic test.
HIV does not spread by touch or physical contact; it spreads only through body fluids.
NACO (National AIDS Control Organisation) leads AIDS prevention efforts in India.
World AIDS Day is observed on 1 December.

formulas.meaning: How HIV converts its RNA genome into DNA that integrates into the host genome.

topics.neet_tip: Typical questions cover the sequence of HIV infection (macrophage, then TH cell), the role of reverse transcriptase and the ELISA test.

topics.explanation: Adolescence, roughly 12-18 years, is the period of physical and psychological transition from childhood to maturity. Curiosity, peer pressure and stress make adolescents vulnerable to drugs, alcohol and tobacco. Opioids bind opioid receptors in the CNS and gastrointestinal tract. Heroin (smack, diacetylmorphine) is a white, bitter powder made by acetylation of morphine, which comes from the latex of the poppy Papaver somniferum. Heroin is a depressant that slows body functions. Morphine is a strong sedative and painkiller used after surgery. Cannabinoids (marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja) come from Cannabis sativa, act on cannabinoid receptors in the brain and affect the cardiovascular system. Cocaine (coke, crack) comes from Erythroxylum coca, interferes with dopamine transport and is a stimulant causing euphoria and increased energy. Atropa belladonna and Datura are hallucinogenic plants. Tobacco nicotine stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and noradrenaline, raising blood pressure and heart rate. Smoking raises blood carbon monoxide, which reduces oxygen carried by haemoglobin. It is linked to lung, bladder and throat cancer, bronchitis, emphysema and coronary heart disease. Chronic alcohol use damages the nervous system and the liver, causing cirrhosis.
key_points: Heroin is made from morphine; morphine comes from the poppy Papaver somniferum.
Cocaine comes from Erythroxylum coca and acts on dopamine transport, stimulating the CNS.
Cannabinoids come from Cannabis sativa; they are usually smoked or taken orally.
Barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and LSD have medical uses for depression and insomnia but are often misused.
Tobacco is smoked, chewed or used as snuff; chewing increases the risk of oral cancer.
Withdrawal symptoms include anxiety, shakiness, nausea and sweating.
Anabolic steroids in females: masculinisation, aggressiveness, mood swings and abnormal menstrual cycles.
Anabolic steroids in females also cause excess hair growth, enlarged clitoris and a deeper voice.
Anabolic steroids in males: acne, reduced testicle size, reduced sperm, kidney and liver problems, breast enlargement and premature baldness.
Prevention: avoid undue peer pressure, education and counselling, help from parents and peers, and attention to danger signs.
topics.neet_tip: Plant-source to drug matching, the receptor or action of each drug, and the effect of nicotine on adrenaline are favourite questions.
topics.topic: Adolescence; drug, alcohol and tobacco abuse

topics.explanation: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) such as Lactobacillus convert milk into curd by producing acids that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins. LAB also increase vitamin B12 and check disease-causing microbes in the stomach. Dough for bread is leavened by baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, whose CO2 makes it puff up. Dosa and idli batters are fermented by bacteria. Toddy is made by fermenting palm sap. Swiss cheese has large holes because Propionibacterium sharmanii produces a lot of CO2. Roquefort cheese is ripened by a specific fungus. In industry, microbes are grown in large vessels called fermenters. Brewer's yeast (S. cerevisiae) ferments malted cereals and fruit juices to make wine and beer without distillation, and whisky, brandy and rum with distillation. Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the mould Penicillium notatum, which inhibited Staphylococci. Chain and Florey established it as an effective antibiotic, and the three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize. Microbes also produce organic acids, enzymes and bioactive molecules.
key_points: Citric acid is produced by Aspergillus niger (fungus).
Acetic acid is produced by Acetobacter aceti (bacterium).
Butyric acid is produced by Clostridium butylicum (bacterium).
Lactic acid is produced by Lactobacillus (bacterium).
Ethanol is produced commercially by Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
Lipases are added to detergents to remove oily stains.
Pectinases and proteases are used to clarify bottled fruit juices.
Streptokinase, from Streptococcus and genetically modified, is a clot buster for myocardial infarction.
Cyclosporin A, from the fungus Trichoderma polysporum, is an immunosuppressant used in organ transplants.
Statins, from the yeast Monascus purpureus, lower blood cholesterol.
Statins work by competitively inhibiting the enzyme for cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA reductase).

formulas.meaning: Alcoholic fermentation by yeast; the $CO_2$ leavens dough and the ethanol forms the basis of beverages.

topics.neet_tip: Microbe-product-use matching (streptokinase, cyclosporin A, statins and organic acids) appears almost every year.
topics.topic: Microbes in household food processing and industrial production

topics.explanation: Sewage is municipal waste water. It is treated in sewage treatment plants (STPs) in two stages. Primary treatment is physical: debris is removed by sequential filtration, and grit is removed by sedimentation. Settled solids form the primary sludge, and the supernatant is the effluent. Secondary (biological) treatment takes place in aeration tanks. Vigorous aeration lets aerobic microbes grow as flocs, which are masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments in mesh-like structures. The flocs consume organic matter and greatly reduce BOD (biochemical oxygen demand). BOD measures the oxygen microbes need to oxidise the organic matter in one litre of water, so higher BOD means more pollution. The effluent then passes to a settling tank, where the flocs sediment as activated sludge. A small part is returned to the aeration tank as inoculum. The rest goes to anaerobic sludge digesters, where anaerobic bacteria digest it and produce biogas (methane, H2S and CO2). The treated effluent is released into rivers and streams. Biogas is also produced from cattle dung (gobar) by methanogens such as Methanobacterium, which are also found in the cattle rumen and help digest cellulose.
key_points: Primary treatment is physical: filtration and sedimentation.
Secondary treatment is biological: aerobic flocs in aeration tanks reduce BOD.
Activated sludge is partly recycled as inoculum and partly sent to anaerobic digesters.
BOD is an index of organic pollution; greater BOD means greater polluting potential.
The Ganga Action Plan and Yamuna Action Plan were launched by the Ministry of Environment and Forests to treat sewage before it reaches rivers.
Biogas contains mainly methane, with $CO_2$, $H_2S$ and $H_2$.
A biogas plant has a 10-15 feet deep concrete tank fed with slurry of dung and a floating cover that rises as gas accumulates.
Biogas technology in India was developed mainly by IARI and KVIC.

formulas.meaning: Approximate composition of biogas, which is mostly methane; used as fuel for cooking and lighting.

topics.neet_tip: NEET tests the sequence of sewage treatment steps, what flocs and activated sludge are, the meaning of BOD and methanogen examples.
topics.topic: Microbes in sewage treatment and energy generation

topics.explanation: Biocontrol is the use of biological methods instead of chemical pesticides to control plant diseases and pests. It supports organic farming and integrated pest management (IPM). Ladybirds control aphids, and dragonflies control mosquitoes. Spores of Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) are sprayed on plants and eaten by butterfly caterpillars. A toxin released in the larval gut kills the larvae while leaving other insects unharmed. Bt toxin genes have been introduced into plants such as Bt cotton. The free-living fungus Trichoderma, common in root ecosystems, controls many plant pathogens. Baculoviruses, mainly the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus, attack insects and arthropods. They are species-specific and narrow-spectrum, so they do not harm non-target organisms and suit IPM in ecologically sensitive areas. Biofertilizers are organisms that enrich soil nutrients. They include bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria.
key_points: Rhizobium fixes nitrogen in the root nodules of legumes (symbiotic).
Azospirillum and Azotobacter are free-living soil nitrogen fixers.
Mycorrhiza (for example Glomus) helps the plant absorb phosphorus from soil.
Mycorrhizal plants also show resistance to root-borne pathogens and tolerance to salinity and drought.
Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria fix atmospheric nitrogen.
Cyanobacteria are important biofertilizers in paddy fields and also add organic matter to the soil.
Biocontrol reduces dependence on toxic chemicals and protects non-target organisms.

formulas.meaning: Biological nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium, Azotobacter and cyanobacteria, which enriches soil nitrogen.

topics.neet_tip: Questions match organisms to roles, such as Bt for caterpillars, Trichoderma as a fungal biocontrol, Glomus for phosphorus and Anabaena in paddy fields.
topics.topic: Microbes as biocontrol agents and biofertilizers

key_facts: Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant malaria; haemozoin causes the recurring chills and fever every 3-4 days.
The female Anopheles is the vector and definitive host of Plasmodium; fertilisation occurs in the mosquito gut.
Plasmodium sporozoites are stored in the mosquito's salivary glands.
Filariasis is caused by Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi and leads to elephantiasis.
Typhoid is caused by Salmonella typhi and confirmed by the Widal test.
Mary Mallon, nicknamed Typhoid Mary, was a carrier of typhoid.
Pneumonia is caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae.
Common cold is caused by rhinoviruses and does not affect the lungs.
Ringworm fungi: Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton.
Houseflies are mechanical carriers of Entamoeba histolytica.
Dengue and chikungunya are transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.
Interferons are the cytokine barrier of innate immunity.
IgA is abundant in colostrum; IgG crosses the placenta; IgE is involved in allergy.
Bone marrow and thymus are primary lymphoid organs; spleen, lymph nodes and tonsils are secondary.
Peyer's patches and the appendix are also secondary lymphoid organs.
MALT forms about 50 percent of the body's lymphoid tissue.
Hepatitis B vaccine is produced in yeast by recombinant DNA technology.
Alpha-interferon is used in cancer immunotherapy.
HIV infects macrophages first (the HIV factory) and then destroys helper T cells.
The incubation period of AIDS is 5-10 years; it is diagnosed by ELISA.
Heroin (diacetylmorphine) is made by acetylation of morphine from Papaver somniferum.
Cocaine comes from Erythroxylum coca and interferes with dopamine transport.
Nicotine stimulates the adrenal medulla to release adrenaline and noradrenaline.
Propionibacterium sharmanii produces the large holes in Swiss cheese.
Penicillin was discovered by Fleming from Penicillium notatum; Fleming, Chain and Florey shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.
Streptokinase comes from Streptococcus; cyclosporin A from Trichoderma polysporum; statins from Monascus purpureus.
Citric acid comes from Aspergillus niger; acetic acid from Acetobacter aceti; butyric acid from Clostridium butylicum.
Methanobacterium is a methanogen that produces biogas from dung and is also found in the cattle rumen.
Baculoviruses of the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus are species-specific biocontrol agents.
Glomus (mycorrhiza) aids phosphorus uptake; Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria are nitrogen-fixing biofertilizers in paddy fields.
common_traps: Thinking Plasmodium reproduces sexually in human RBCs or liver. In humans it reproduces only asexually; gametocytes form in RBCs, but fertilisation occurs in the mosquito gut.
Calling the thymus or bone marrow a secondary lymphoid organ. They are primary; spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches and MALT are secondary.
Assuming colostrum gives active immunity. It provides ready-made IgA, so the immunity is passive; vaccination gives active immunity.

Confusing the sources of Trichoderma products. Trichoderma polysporum gives cyclosporin A (immunosuppressant), while Trichoderma as a free-living fungus is a biocontrol agent; statins come from Monascus purpureus.
Believing that wine and beer are distilled. They are not distilled; whisky, brandy and rum are distilled.
Thinking HIV first infects helper T cells. It first multiplies in macrophages, which act as the HIV factory, and then enters and destroys TH cells.
Assuming low BOD means polluted water. High BOD indicates high organic pollution; secondary treatment aims to reduce BOD.
Calling heroin a stimulant. Heroin and other opioids are depressants; cocaine is the stimulant.
quick_revision: Malaria: Plasmodium and female Anopheles; asexual in human liver and RBCs, sexual in mosquito gut; haemozoin causes fever.
Other diseases: typhoid (Salmonella typhi, Widal); pneumonia (Streptococcus, Haemophilus); common cold (rhinovirus); ringworm (Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton).
Innate barriers: physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine (interferons); acquired immunity is specific and has memory.
Antibody = $H_2L_2$; IgA in colostrum, IgG crosses placenta, IgE in allergy.
Lymphoid organs: primary = bone marrow and thymus; secondary = spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, MALT.
Cancer: loss of contact inhibition, metastasis; detected by biopsy, CT and MRI; treated by surgery, radiation, chemotherapy and alpha-interferon.
HIV: retrovirus with reverse transcriptase; macrophage then TH cells; 5-10 year incubation; ELISA.
Drugs: heroin and morphine from poppy (depressant); cocaine from Erythroxylum (stimulant, dopamine); cannabinoids from Cannabis sativa.
Food microbes: LAB make curd (vitamin B12); Saccharomyces leavens bread and brews beverages; Propionibacterium makes Swiss cheese holes.
Microbial medicines: streptokinase is a clot buster, cyclosporin A an immunosuppressant, statins lower cholesterol.
Sewage: primary (physical) then secondary (flocs, lower BOD), then activated sludge and anaerobic digesters producing biogas ($CH_4$, $CO_2$, $H_2S$).
Biocontrol: Bt kills caterpillars, Trichoderma controls plant pathogens, Nucleopolyhedrovirus suits IPM; biofertilizers include Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Glomus and Anabaena.
